report:
## Research summary

There is moderate, reasonably good evidence supporting the claim, though it's context-dependent rather than universal.

**Supporting evidence:**
- A DTU-led field intervention study across 29 real bedrooms found that leaving a window (or, to a lesser degree, an interior door) open improved indoor air quality—mainly by lowering CO2 levels—and was associated with better subjective sleep quality and next-day cognitive performance (sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132322008605; dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day).
- Related lab studies show that as bedroom CO2 rises above roughly 900–1350 ppm (which happens when doors/windows are shut, especially with multiple sleepers), sleep quality and next-morning alertness decline. Ventilating to keep CO2 below ~750–800 ppm is linked to no measurable sleep impairment (link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-13-9520-8_99; researchgate.net/publication/375214318_The_Influence_of_Bedroom_CO2_Concentration_on_Sleep_Quality; news-medical.net/news/20251021/Study-offers-a-nuanced-understanding-of-how-bedroom-ventilation-affects-sleep-health.aspx).

**Important caveats:**
- A Shanghai study cited by the Sleep Foundation found that although air quality improved with an open window, actual sleep suffered in summer because rooms became hotter and noisier (sleepfoundation.org/sleep-news/open-window-may-be-better-for-sleep-but-we-keep-it-closed).
- If outdoor air is polluted, cold, humid, or noisy, opening a window can offset or reverse the ventilation benefit (aol.com/lifestyle/open-bedroom-window-winter-better-160000273.html; sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0013935120313037).

## Conclusion

The core mechanism—fresh air lowers CO2/staleness and this helps sleep and next-day function—is supported by controlled research, so your sister's general instinct is scientifically grounded. However, the benefit is conditional: it depends on outdoor air quality, temperature, humidity, and noise levels. In noisy, polluted, or extreme-temperature environments, opening a window may do more harm than good, so it's not a universal rule but a generally reasonable practice when conditions allow.
